architectural_implications.after: A single system-level objective is defined, and component metrics are derived from and scored against it.
architectural_implications.before: Each subsystem/agent is tuned against its own local metric; global behavior is an emergent side effect.
architectural_implications.consequence: Prevents locally optimal but globally degraded configurations; requires instrumentation that ties component behavior to end-to-end outcomes.
architectural_implications.observation: Optimization is being applied per component rather than per system.

architectural_implications.after: Interfaces expose roughly 6-7 elements, with internals hidden, and the same chunking rule reapplied recursively at each hierarchy level.
architectural_implications.before: Interfaces and context dumps expose many elements; internals leak across boundaries.
architectural_implications.consequence: Lower context load for both human reviewers and models; more stable, composable boundaries.
architectural_implications.observation: Abstraction surfaces are sized organically rather than to a working-memory budget.

architectural_implications.after: Situation understanding and problem formulation become explicit, measured stages preceding solution activity.
architectural_implications.before: Systems are validated by completing prescribed lifecycle steps; front-end problem formulation is absent from the standards.
architectural_implications.consequence: Evaluation must score intent alignment, not just pipeline step completion, otherwise process-compliant failures pass certification.
architectural_implications.observation: Process conformance is treated as a proxy for success.

architectural_implications.after: Pure (cognitive framing), applied (activity), and domain layers are separated with distinct evaluation.
architectural_implications.before: The same function both frames the problem and executes requirements/architecting/V&V activities.
architectural_implications.consequence: Problem-framing quality can be improved and measured independently of procedural execution quality.
architectural_implications.observation: Cognition and activity are bundled into one role.

article_ideas.angle: Take the standard-following practitioner who fails on intent as the canonical failure, then map it onto agent pipelines that pass workflow checks while missing user goals, and argue for splitting intent elicitation out as a scored gate preceding solution work.
article_ideas.audience: AI evaluation engineers, agent platform architects, systems engineering leads
article_ideas.based_on: George follows standards meticulously but fails because he cannot understand what the customer really wants.
article_ideas.thesis: Evaluation harnesses and lifecycle standards that score procedural conformance can certify systems that never understood the situation; front-end problem formulation must be a measured stage with its own intent-alignment score, or process-compliance becomes a false quality signal.
article_ideas.title: Process Conformance Is Not Intent Alignment: Why Passing Every Step Still Fails the User

article_ideas.angle: Treat per-component KPI tuning — accuracy, latency, token budget — as an anti-pattern, show why emergent global behavior is an unchecked side effect of local tuning, and specify the instrumentation needed to score components against end-to-end outcomes.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework builders, MLOps and platform engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Optimizing subsystems independently does not lead to a system optimum
article_ideas.thesis: Independently tuning each agent or tool against its own metric converges to a local optimum that can be worse than the untuned whole; the system-level objective must be the single optimization target and component metrics must be derived from it, not optimized alongside it.
article_ideas.title: The Optimization Paradox in Decomposed AI Pipelines: When Tuning Every Agent Makes the System Worse

article_ideas.angle: Contrast diagnostic decomposition with generative context modeling, and show why agent systems that reuse their debugging decomposition for planning produce plan sets that never include the missing environmental interaction.
article_ideas.based_on: Conventional thinking does not explain where solutions come from.
article_ideas.thesis: Decomposition is a diagnostic tool for explaining and debugging existing behavior, but it does not tell you where solutions come from; generating candidate solutions requires modeling the whole system in its environment and its interactions with adjacent systems, so debugging and planning deserve separate architectures.
article_ideas.title: Decomposition Explains, Context Generates: Splitting Analysis From Solution Finding

article_ideas.angle: Convert Miller's Rule into numbers for tool schemas, sub-agent interface descriptions, and context packing, and confront the cost: what fails below a hidden boundary is invisible to review conducted at that level.
article_ideas.audience: Tool/API designers, prompt and context engineers
article_ideas.based_on: Partitioning a complex diagram into six systems and hiding internal details to reduce complexity.
article_ideas.thesis: If abstraction boundaries are sized to a consumer's working-memory limit and recursively reapplied, then interface surfaces should expose on the order of six to seven elements with internals hidden — a concrete, testable design budget rather than a vague call to manage complexity.
article_ideas.title: Size Your Interfaces to Seven: Chunking as an Engineering Budget for Tool Schemas and Context

source.author: Joseph Kasser
source.title: Systems thinking as it applies to systems engineering

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Prof Joseph E Kasser
  • Channel: Joseph Kasser
  • Main topic: Systems thinking, holistic thinking perspectives, and systems engineering education and practice
  • Purpose: To challenge traditional systems engineering paradigms, introduce holistic thinking perspectives, and provide a framework for improving systems engineering education and practice. Prof Joseph E Kasser presents a critical examination of traditional systems engineering, arguing that it relies on a flawed paradigm rooted in conventional reductionist thinking rather than true systems thinking. Through frameworks like the Holistic Thinking Perspectives (HTP) and the Hitchins-Kasser-Massie Framework (HKMF), Kasser explains how systems engineering is often taught and practiced incorrectly, focusing on process and tools rather than understanding problematic situations and capturing emergent system behavior.

Topic Map

Apologies and Warning

  • Explanation: Introduction to the presentation, warning that it presents traditional systems engineering in a different paradigm that may challenge or offend conventional views.
  • Key claims:
    • Traditional systems engineering is viewed through a different paradigm.
    • The talk is designed to make you think and take you out of your comfort zone.
    • Some information may be dated due to years of accumulated research.
  • Examples:
    • Presentations based on 20 years of research and earlier slides.
  • Terminology:
    • Traditional systems engineering
    • Paradigm
    • Holistic thinking
  • Why it matters: Establishes the critical tone and unorthodox perspective of the presentation.

Problem-Solving: Conventional vs. Systems Thinking

  • Explanation: Contrasts conventional thinking, which isolates parts to understand behavior, with systems thinking, which explores the emergent nature of the system as a whole.
  • Key claims:
    • Conventional thinking isolates parts to understand behavior.
    • Systems thinking explores emergent properties of the whole system and its interactions with adjacent systems.
    • Conventional thinking does not explain where solutions come from.
  • Examples:
    • A car not starting on a cold winter morning; conventional thinking looks for a dead battery, while systems thinking examines the car in its environment and traffic context.
  • Terminology:
    • Conventional thinking
    • Systems thinking
    • Emergent nature
    • Adjacent systems
  • Why it matters: Highlights the fundamental difference in how problems are approached under different mindsets.

The Holistic Thinking Perspectives (HTP)

  • Explanation: Presents nine holistic thinking perspectives derived from research and Barry Richmond's seven streams of system thinking, categorized into external, internal, progressive, quantitative, and scientific.
  • Key claims:
    • There are nine holistic thinking perspectives analogous to the blind men and the elephant parable.
    • External perspectives cover big picture and operational views.
    • Internal perspectives cover functional and structural views (analysis).
    • Progressive perspectives cover generic, continuum, and temporal views.
    • Quantitative and scientific perspectives complete the set.
  • Examples:
    • Applying the nine perspectives to a camera (big picture, operational, functional, structural, generic, continuum, temporal, quantitative, scientific).
  • Terminology:
    • Holistic Thinking Perspectives
    • Big Picture
    • Operational
    • Functional
    • Structural
    • Generic
    • Continuum
    • Temporal
    • Quantitative
    • Scientific
  • Why it matters: Provides a comprehensive framework for viewing systems from multiple angles to achieve full understanding.

The Principle of Hierarchies and Optimization Paradox

  • Explanation: Discusses Miller's Law (7 plus or minus 2 objects), fractal hierarchies, and the systems optimization paradox regarding optimizing subsystems vs. the whole system.
  • Key claims:
    • The human brain can only hold about 7 plus or minus 2 objects at once (Miller's Rule).
    • Hierarchies are fractal; systems are subsystems of larger systems.
    • Optimizing subsystems independently does not lead to a system optimum; you must optimize the system as a whole.
  • Examples:
    • Partitioning a complex diagram into six systems and hiding internal details to reduce complexity.
  • Terminology:
    • Miller's Rule
    • Fractal hierarchies
    • Systems optimization paradox
    • Subsystem optimization
  • Why it matters: Explains how to manage complexity by dealing with appropriate hierarchical levels.

Systems Engineering Education and Standards

  • Explanation: Critiques how systems engineering is taught in academia and defined in standards (MIL-STD-499, EIA-632, IEEE-1220, CMMI, ISO-15288), arguing they focus on management and process rather than problem formulation.
  • Key claims:
    • Academic courses focus on parts, lecture-based learning, and process rather than how-to problem solving.
    • Standards like DoD Directive 5000 and EIA-632 focus on managing the process (management of systems engineering) rather than doing systems engineering.
    • Early stages of problem formulation and conceptualization are missing from standards.
  • Examples:
    • The 'egg' process diagram and Waterfall lifecycle models showing lack of front-end problem exploration.
  • Terminology:
    • Systems engineering education
    • SEDC
    • DoD 5000
    • EIA-632
    • IEEE-1220
    • Waterfall lifecycle
  • Why it matters: Identifies root causes of project failures and educational gaps in the discipline.

Pure, Applied, and Domain Systems Engineering (SETA)

  • Explanation: Defines Systems Engineering The Activity (SETA) and categorizes it into pure systems engineering (cognitive skills), applied systems engineering (activities like requirements and V&V), and domain systems engineering.
  • Key claims:
    • Systems engineering is analogous to mathematics (pure and applied).
    • Pure systems engineering involves cognitive skills and systems thinking.
    • Applied systems engineering involves activities like requirements management, architecting, and V&V.
    • Domain systems engineering applies these in specific fields.
  • Examples:
    • Traffic congestion problem: problem domain (traffic management), solution domain (subway system), implementation domain (tunnel boring).
  • Terminology:
    • SETA
    • Pure systems engineering
    • Applied systems engineering
    • Domain systems engineering
  • Why it matters: Clarifies the nature of systems engineering activity and resolves confusion in definitions.

Types of Systems Engineers and George's Dilemma

  • Explanation: Categorizes systems engineers into five types based on capabilities (from problem causer to innovator-leader) and illustrates the plight of a nominal 'good' systems engineer (George) trapped in the B-paradigm.
  • Key claims:
    • There are five types of systems engineers: Type I (problem causer), Type II (apprentice doer), Type III (problem solver), Type IV (problem formulator), Type V (innovator-leader).
    • George follows standards meticulously but fails because he cannot understand what the customer really wants.
    • Outstanding systems engineers use holistic models (CONOPS) and consider system-generic requirements.
  • Examples:
    • George reading hundreds of customer requirements, creating hierarchical models using MBSE tools, yet failing because requirements keep changing.
  • Terminology:
    • Five types of systems engineers
    • A-paradigm
    • B-paradigm
    • CONOPS
    • System-generic requirements
  • Why it matters: Explains why projects fail despite following standard processes and highlights the superiority of outstanding systems engineers.

The Hitchins-Kasser-Massie Framework (HKMF)

  • Explanation: Introduces the HKMF matrix combining Hitchins' five layers (product, system, business, supply chain, socio-economic) with lifecycle phases to analyze systems engineering education and practice.
  • Key claims:
    • Systems engineering practice is heavily concentrated in layer 2 (system) and phases B-F (requirements, design, integration), ignoring layer 3-5 and front-end/operations.
    • Many systems engineering master's degrees do not require a single systems engineering course.
    • Traditional processes treat systems engineering as a white box while operations treat it as a black box.
  • Examples:
    • HKMF area coverage analysis showing gaps in academic curricula and standards.
  • Terminology:
    • HKMF
    • Hitchins layers
    • Lifecycle phases
    • White box vs. black box
  • Why it matters: Provides an analytical tool to evaluate educational curricula and professional practices.

Conclusion, Situation Awareness States, and Lessons Learned

  • Explanation: Summarizes key takeaways, presents a situation awareness state diagram (from unaware to changing the situation), and offers advice on becoming an outstanding systems engineer.
  • Key claims:
    • Conclusions and inferences are only as good as your domain knowledge.
    • Communications and risk management are key to success.

Prof Joseph E Kasser presents a critical examination of traditional systems engineering, arguing that it relies on a flawed paradigm rooted in conventional reductionist thinking rather than true systems thinking. Through frameworks like the Holistic Thinking Perspectives (HTP) and the Hitchins-Kasser-Massie Framework (HKMF), Kasser explains how systems engineering is often taught and practiced incorrectly, focusing on process and tools rather than understanding problematic situations and capturing emergent system behavior.

### Apologies and Warning
- **Explanation**: Introduction to the presentation, warning that it presents traditional systems engineering in a different paradigm that may challenge or offend conventional views.
- **Key claims**:
  - Traditional systems engineering is viewed through a different paradigm.
  - The talk is designed to make you think and take you out of your comfort zone.
  - Some information may be dated due to years of accumulated research.
- **Examples**:
  - Presentations based on 20 years of research and earlier slides.
- **Terminology**:
  - Traditional systems engineering
  - Paradigm
  - Holistic thinking
- **Why it matters**: Establishes the critical tone and unorthodox perspective of the presentation.
### Problem-Solving: Conventional vs. Systems Thinking
- **Explanation**: Contrasts conventional thinking, which isolates parts to understand behavior, with systems thinking, which explores the emergent nature of the system as a whole.
- **Key claims**:
  - Conventional thinking isolates parts to understand behavior.
  - Systems thinking explores emergent properties of the whole system and its interactions with adjacent systems.
  - Conventional thinking does not explain where solutions come from.
- **Examples**:
  - A car not starting on a cold winter morning; conventional thinking looks for a dead battery, while systems thinking examines the car in its environment and traffic context.
- **Terminology**:
  - Conventional thinking
  - Systems thinking
  - Emergent nature
  - Adjacent systems
- **Why it matters**: Highlights the fundamental difference in how problems are approached under different mindsets.
### The Holistic Thinking Perspectives (HTP)
- **Explanation**: Presents nine holistic thinking perspectives derived from research and Barry Richmond's seven streams of system thinking, categorized into external, internal, progressive, quantitative, and scientific.
- **Key claims**:
  - There are nine holistic thinking perspectives analogous to the blind men and the elephant parable.
  - External perspectives cover big picture and operational views.
  - Internal perspectives cover functional and structural views (analysis).
  - Progressive perspectives cover generic, continuum, and temporal views.
  - Quantitative and scientific perspectives complete the set.
- **Examples**:
  - Applying the nine perspectives to a camera (big picture, operational, functional, structural, generic, continuum, temporal, quantitative, scientific).
- **Terminology**:
  - Holistic Thinking Perspectives
  - Big Picture
  - Operational
  - Functional
  - Structural
  - Generic
  - Continuum
  - Temporal
  - Quantitative
  - Scientific
- **Why it matters**: Provides a comprehensive framework for viewing systems from multiple angles to achieve full understanding.
### The Principle of Hierarchies and Optimization Paradox
- **Explanation**: Discusses Miller's Law (7 plus or minus 2 objects), fractal hierarchies, and the systems optimization paradox regarding optimizing subsystems vs. the whole system.
- **Key claims**:
  - The human brain can only hold about 7 plus or minus 2 objects at once (Miller's Rule).
  - Hierarchies are fractal; systems are subsystems of larger systems.
  - Optimizing subsystems independently does not lead to a system optimum; you must optimize the system as a whole.
- **Examples**:
  - Partitioning a complex diagram into six systems and hiding internal details to reduce complexity.
- **Terminology**:
  - Miller's Rule
  - Fractal hierarchies
  - Systems optimization paradox
  - Subsystem optimization
- **Why it matters**: Explains how to manage complexity by dealing with appropriate hierarchical levels.
### Systems Engineering Education and Standards
- **Explanation**: Critiques how systems engineering is taught in academia and defined in standards (MIL-STD-499, EIA-632, IEEE-1220, CMMI, ISO-15288), arguing they focus on management and process rather than problem formulation.
- **Key claims**:
  - Academic courses focus on parts, lecture-based learning, and process rather than how-to problem solving.
  - Standards like DoD Directive 5000 and EIA-632 focus on managing the process (management of systems engineering) rather than doing systems engineering.
  - Early stages of problem formulation and conceptualization are missing from standards.
- **Examples**:
  - The 'egg' process diagram and Waterfall lifecycle models showing lack of front-end problem exploration.
- **Terminology**:
  - Systems engineering education
  - SEDC
  - DoD 5000
  - EIA-632
  - IEEE-1220
  - Waterfall lifecycle
- **Why it matters**: Identifies root causes of project failures and educational gaps in the discipline.
### Pure, Applied, and Domain Systems Engineering (SETA)
- **Explanation**: Defines Systems Engineering The Activity (SETA) and categorizes it into pure systems engineering (cognitive skills), applied systems engineering (activities like requirements and V&V), and domain systems engineering.
- **Key claims**:
  - Systems engineering is analogous to mathematics (pure and applied).
  - Pure systems engineering involves cognitive skills and systems thinking.
  - Applied systems engineering involves activities like requirements management, architecting, and V&V.
  - Domain systems engineering applies these in specific fields.
- **Examples**:
  - Traffic congestion problem: problem domain (traffic management), solution domain (subway system), implementation domain (tunnel boring).
- **Terminology**:
  - SETA
  - Pure systems engineering
  - Applied systems engineering
  - Domain systems engineering
- **Why it matters**: Clarifies the nature of systems engineering activity and resolves confusion in definitions.
### Types of Systems Engineers and George's Dilemma
- **Explanation**: Categorizes systems engineers into five types based on capabilities (from problem causer to innovator-leader) and illustrates the plight of a nominal 'good' systems engineer (George) trapped in the B-paradigm.
- **Key claims**:
  - There are five types of systems engineers: Type I (problem causer), Type II (apprentice doer), Type III (problem solver), Type IV (problem formulator), Type V (innovator-leader).
  - George follows standards meticulously but fails because he cannot understand what the customer really wants.
  - Outstanding systems engineers use holistic models (CONOPS) and consider system-generic requirements.

  - A-paradigm
  - B-paradigm
  - CONOPS
  - System-generic requirements
- **Why it matters**: Explains why projects fail despite following standard processes and highlights the superiority of outstanding systems engineers.

- **Examples**:

  - Lifecycle phases
  - White box vs. black box
- **Why it matters**: Provides an analytical tool to evaluate educational curricula and professional practices.
